title: Practical Vipassana Exercises
excerpt: By Venerable Mahasi Sayadaw of Myanmar; translated by Lin Wurui.

inline.s: By Venerable Mahasi Sayadaw of Myanmar
, translated by Lin Wurui

blocks.text: 1. Awareness of Mental and Physical Phenomena

inline.s: To practice insight meditation is to endeavor to understand correctly the mental and physical phenomena that occur within oneself. The physical phenomena are those that everyone can clearly perceive. The body that each person perceives is composed of a group of material qualities (called rūpa). The mental or psychological phenomena are the activities of consciousness or awareness (called nāma). To clearly perceive these mental and physical phenomena (together called nāma-rūpa), one may, at the very moment of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, or thinking, perceive them through observation and give them attention (or note them): “seeing, seeing,” “hearing, hearing,” “smelling, smelling,” “tasting, tasting,” “touching, touching,” “thinking, thinking.”

Each time he sees, hears, smells, tastes, touches, or thinks, he should give attention to (or note) that fact. But a beginner cannot possibly note every phenomenon that occurs, so he must begin by noting those phenomena that are conspicuous and easy to observe.

With each breath, the abdomen rises and falls; this movement is always conspicuous, and it is a material quality called the air element (or wind element). One should begin by noting this movement, observing the abdomen with the mind. When you breathe in, you will notice the abdomen rising; when you breathe out, it falls. As the abdomen rises, note inwardly “rising”; as it falls, note inwardly “falling.” If the movement is not clear, you may place your hand on the abdomen. But do not change the breathing; do not deliberately slow or quicken the breath, and do not breathe too forcefully. If you change the breathing, you will become tired. Breathe naturally, and note the rising and falling movement of the abdomen. Give attention (or note) with the mind, not by reciting with the mouth.

(Editor's note: There are two common ways of breathing: chest breathing and abdominal breathing. Chest breathing relies mainly on the movement of the ribs and breastbone; on inhalation the chest expands in width and depth. Since air enters the lungs directly during this kind of breathing, the chest expands while the abdomen remains flat. The breathing in this article uses the natural method of abdominal breathing — that is, on inhalation the abdominal muscles gently expand (the abdomen rises), and on exhalation they gently contract (the abdomen falls). Compared with chest breathing, this method of breathing brings far more benefits to bodily health.)

In insight meditation, the name and the saying are not important; what truly matters is to know and to be aware. In noting the rising of the abdomen, one must follow it from the very beginning of the movement to the end of the whole rising process, as if seeing it with one's own eyes. The same applies to noting the falling movement. When noting the rising movement, keep the aware mind in step with the rising movement, so that the movement and the awareness are synchronized, like a stone thrown to hit its target squarely. The same applies to the falling movement.

While noting the movement of the abdomen, the mind may wander here and there. At that point, note inwardly: “wandering, wandering.” After noting it once or twice, the wandering mind will stop, and then we return to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen. If the mind is found to have arrived somewhere, note “arriving, arriving,” and then return to the movement of the abdomen. If the thought of meeting someone arises, note “meeting, meeting,” and then return to the rising and falling of the abdomen. If you think of someone and speak with him, note “speaking, speaking.”

In short, whenever any thought or recollection arises, it must be given attention (or noted). If you imagine, note “imagining.” If you think, note “thinking.” If you plan, note “planning.” If you perceive, note “perceiving.” If you reflect, note “reflecting.” If you feel happy, note “happy.” If you feel bored, note “bored.” If you feel joyful, note “joyful.” If you feel discouraged, note “discouraged.” Noting all these activities of the mind is called “contemplation of mind” (cittānupassanā).

Because we do not note these mental activities, we identify them with a “person” or an “individual.” We imagine that the one who imagines, thinks, plans, and perceives is “I,” and that there is “a person” who has been living and thinking continuously since childhood. In reality, no such person exists; there are only these unceasing mental activities. Therefore, we should note these mental activities and know what they are. This is why we must note the arising of every mental activity.
When it is given attention, it disappears.
Then we return to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen.

After sitting in meditation for a long time, there will be sensations of stiffness and heat in the body; these too must be carefully noted. Likewise, there are sensations of pain and fatigue. All these sensations are feelings of suffering (dukkha vedanā), and noting these feelings is “contemplation of feelings” (vedanānupassanā). Not knowing or neglecting to note these feelings, you will think, “I feel stiff, I feel hot, I feel pain. A moment ago I was fine, and now I am uncomfortable because of these unpleasant feelings,” identifying these feelings with a “self.” This is a wrong view. In reality, no “I” is involved; there is only one unpleasant “feeling” after another arising continuously.

These are like fresh, unceasing currents of electricity flowing to a lamp. Whenever there is an unpleasant contact in the body, feelings of suffering arise one after another. These feelings should be carefully noted, whether they are feelings of stiffness, heat, or pain. When a beginner starts to practice, these feelings seem so strong that there arises the desire to change posture; this “desire” should be noted, and then one should return to noting the feelings of stiffness, heat, and so on.

Patience leads to nibbāna” — this saying is most fitting when applied to earnest meditation. One must be patient during meditation. If, unable to bear sensations of stiffness or heat, one keeps moving or changing posture, concentration (samādhi) cannot arise; and if concentration cannot be developed, wisdom cannot be obtained, nor the path-fruit and nibbāna that lead to nibbāna. This is why patience is needed during meditation. What most requires patience are the unpleasant sensations in the body, such as stiffness, heat, and pain, as well as other sensations that are hard to bear. The meditator should not give up meditation and change posture the moment these sensations arise. He should continue patiently noting “stiff, stiff” or “hot, hot.” If he notes them patiently, these moderate sensations will disappear. When attention is strong and concentrated, even very strong sensations will disappear. Then he returns to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen.

If, after noting for some time, the sensation still does not disappear, or if the sensation becomes unbearable, then of course one must change posture. At that moment one should begin noting: “wishing to change, wishing to change.” If the hand is raised, note “raising, raising”; if the hand is moved, note “moving, moving.” Change these postures gently, noting: “raising, raising,” “moving, moving,” and “touching, touching.”

If the body sways, note “swaying, swaying”; if the foot is lifted, note “lifting, lifting”; if it is moved, note “moving, moving”; if it is put down, note “putting down, putting down.” If there is no change and one is simply resting still, return to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen. There must be no gap between one noting and the next; only one noting following another, one concentration following another, one wisdom following another. Only in this way can the meditator's wisdom continue and mature step by step. Only through this kind of accumulated momentum can the wisdom of the path and fruition be attained. The process of meditation is like rubbing two sticks together without ceasing in order to obtain the heat needed to kindle a fire.

Likewise, in insight meditation, the noting (or labeling) should be continuous without any gap, whatever phenomenon arises. For example, if an unbearable itching sensation arises and one wishes to scratch, the meditator should note this “feeling” and the “desire” to scratch, and should not immediately scratch directly in order to remove the itching.

If one notes continuously, the itching sensation will gradually disappear, and the meditator can return to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen. If the itching sensation does not actually disappear, then of course one may scratch to remove it, but beforehand one must note the “desire” to scratch. All the movements of removing the itch must be noted, especially the movements of “touching,” “pulling,” “pushing,” and “scratching,” and finally one returns to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen.

Each time one changes posture, first note the intention or desire to change, then carefully note every movement, such as rising from the sitting posture, raising the hand, moving it, extending it. The change of posture and the noting mind should be in harmony. When the body sways forward, note it. When rising, the body becomes light and rises; place the mind on these movements, gently noting (or labeling) “rising, rising.”

The meditator should comport himself like a feeble person. A healthy person rises easily, quickly, or abruptly. Not so a feeble person, who rises slowly and gently. The same with a person suffering from back pain, who needs to rise slowly to reduce the pain in his back.

So too the meditator should move slowly and gently when changing posture, for only thus can there be good mindfulness, concentration, and insight. Therefore, at the beginning, movements should be gentle and slow. When rising, the meditator should move gently, like a feeble person, noting at the same time “rising, rising.” Moreover, what is seen with the eyes should be treated as though it had not been seen; so too with what is heard with the ears. During meditation, the meditator concerns himself only with noting, and need not attend to what is seen or heard. Therefore, whether he sees or hears something strange or conspicuous, he should treat it as though he had not seen or heard it, and simply note carefully.

When moving the body, the meditator should move slowly, like a feeble person, gently moving the hands and feet, bending or straightening them, lowering or raising the head — all these movements should be gentle. When rising from the sitting posture, he should move slowly, noting “rising, rising.” When straightening the body and standing, note “standing, standing”; when looking around, note “looking, looking.” When walking, note whether the step is left or right, and be aware of all the continuous movements from the lifting of the foot to the placing of it down. Noting each step as right foot or left foot is the way one should note when walking fast. When walking fast or walking a long distance, it is enough to note in this way.
(The above concerns sitting meditation.)

blocks.text: 6. Walking, Standing, Sitting, and Lying Down

inline.s: 1. As for walking slowly, or walking back and forth in walking meditation, three stages should be noted in each step: lifting the foot, moving the foot forward, and putting it down. One should begin by noting the movements of lifting and putting down the foot. When lifting the foot, be clearly aware of it; when putting it down, likewise be clearly aware of the heavy sensation of placing it down.

When walking, one should note the “lifting” and “putting down” of each step; after about two days, this noting will become easy. After that, note the three stages: “lifting, moving forward, putting down.” At the beginning, it is enough to note only one or two stages: when walking fast, note only “right step, left step”; when walking slowly, note “lifting, putting down.” If, while walking, one wishes to sit down, note “wishing to sit, wishing to sit.” When sitting down, concentrate on the heavy sensation of the body sitting down.

After sitting down, note the movements of arranging the hands and feet. When there are no such movements and the body is still, note the rising and falling of the abdomen. While noting thus, if sensations of stiffness and heat arise in the limbs, note them. Then return to the “rising, falling” of the abdomen. If at this time the desire to lie down arises, note it, and when lying down, note the movements of the feet and hands. The raising of the hand, the moving of the hand, the elbow touching the floor, the shifting of the body, the stretching of the legs, the leaning of the body as one slowly prepares to lie down — all these movements must be given attention.
It is important to give attention when lying down. During the process of this movement (when lying down), special wisdom (path knowledge and fruition knowledge) can be attained.
When concentration and wisdom are strong, this wisdom may arise at any moment; it may arise while bending an arm or while stretching one out. This is how Venerable Ānanda attained arahantship.

Venerable Ānanda strove valiantly, wishing to attain arahantship on the eve of the first council for the compilation of the Dharma. He practiced the insight method of contemplation of the body throughout the whole night, noting his steps: right and left, lifting, moving forward, putting down; noting the arising of phenomena one after another: the desire to walk and the movements of the body while walking. Although he practiced without ceasing until nearly dawn, he still could not attain the fruit of arahantship. He realized that he had practiced walking meditation to excess. In order to balance concentration and effort, he should practice lying-down meditation for a while, so he entered his chamber. He sat on the bed, then lay down. As he did so, noting “lying down, lying down,” he instantly attained the fruit of arahantship.

Before lying down, Venerable Ānanda was only a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). From the stage of stream-enterer, he continued to practice meditation, attaining in succession the fruit of once-returner (sakadāgāmin), the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin), and the fruit of arahant. In only a few moments he attained these three successive fruits.
Try to keep in mind this example of Venerable Ānanda's attainment of arahantship. Such realization can occur at any time; it does not require a long time.
This is why the meditator must note diligently at every moment.

Do not relax your attention, and do not think that “this little bit of slackness will not matter much.” All movements — including how the hands and feet are placed when lying down — must be noted carefully and without the slightest relaxation. If there is no movement and one is still, return to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen. Even if it is late and time to sleep, one must not cease noting. A serious and earnestly striving meditator must keep up mindfulness at all times, as though he could forgo sleep, continuing to meditate until he falls asleep. If the meditation is going well, he will not fall asleep. If he is drowsy, he will fall asleep. When he wishes to sleep, he should note “wishing to sleep, wishing to sleep”; if the eyelids droop, note “drooping, drooping”; if the eyelids feel heavy, note “heavy”; if the eyes feel sore, note “sore.” By noting in this way, the drowsiness may disappear and the eyes become “bright.” Then the meditator should note “bright, bright,” and continue to return to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen.

But although the meditator persists in continuing to meditate, if real sleepiness invades him, he will fall asleep. Sleeping is not a difficult matter; in fact it is an easy one. If one meditates lying down, one will gradually feel drowsy and then fall asleep. This is why a beginner should not practice lying-down meditation too much; he should practice more sitting and walking meditation. But if it is late and time to sleep, he should practice lying-down meditation, noting the rising and falling of the abdomen, and he will fall asleep naturally.

The time a meditator sleeps is his time of rest, but a serious meditator should limit his sleep to four hours. This is the “midnight period” set by the Buddha. Four hours of sleep is enough. If a beginner feels that four hours is not enough for his health, he may extend it to five or six hours. Six hours of sleep is clearly sufficient for health.

As soon as the meditator wakes up, he should immediately resume noting. A meditator who truly strives, wishing to attain path knowledge and fruition knowledge, rests only while asleep; during all other waking hours he notes continuously without rest. Therefore, as soon as he wakes, he should note the waking state of mind as “waking, waking.” If he cannot yet perceive it in this way, he should begin noting the rising and falling of the abdomen. If he wishes to get up from bed, he should note “wishing to get up, wishing to get up,” and then continue to note the movements of moving the hands and feet. When he raises his head and gets up, note “getting up, getting up”; when he sits down, note “sitting, sitting”; and when arranging the hands and feet, whatever movements there are, note all of them. If there are no such movements and he is simply sitting still, note the rising and falling of the abdomen.

Attention should also be given when washing the face and bathing; because these movements are relatively quick, one should try to note as many movements as possible. Also, the movements of dressing, making the bed, opening the door, closing the door, and the like should be noted as carefully as possible.

When the meditator eats and looks at the table, he should note “looking, looking.” Reaching out the hand to take food, touching the food, picking it up, bringing it to the mouth, lowering the head and putting the food into the mouth, lowering the arm, and raising the head again — all these movements should be given timely attention.
(Note: The manner of noting here follows the way Burmese people eat. Those who use knives and forks, spoons, or chopsticks should also note each movement in the appropriate manner.)

When chewing food, note “chewing, chewing”; when the taste of the food is known, note “knowing, knowing”; when tasting the food and swallowing, and when the food passes down the throat, note all that occurs. This is how the meditator should note as he eats mouthful by mouthful. When taking soup, all the movements — reaching out the hand, holding the spoon, and scooping the soup — should be noted. It is rather difficult to note these movements while eating, because there are so many movements to observe and note. A beginner may miss some of the movements that should be noted, but he should resolve to note everything. Of course he may miss some, but as his concentration strengthens, he will be able to note everything that occurs.

Well then, I have mentioned so many things for the meditator to note; but, in brief, there are only a few things to note. When walking fast, note “right step, left step”; when walking slowly, note “lifting, putting down”; when sitting still, simply note the rising and falling of the abdomen; when lying down, if there is nothing special to note, likewise note the rising and falling of the abdomen. While noting, if the mind wanders this way and that, note the arising of mental activities, then return to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen. When sensations of stiffness, pain, and itching arise, note these feelings, then return to the rising and falling of the abdomen. When the limbs bend, stretch, and move; when the head lowers and lifts; when the body sways and straightens — note all these, then return to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen.

As the meditator continues to note, he will be able to note the arising of more and more phenomena. At the beginning, with his mind wandering here and there, he may miss many things. But he need not be discouraged; every beginner encounters these same difficulties. As he practices longer, he will become aware of every stray thought, until finally no more idle thoughts remain in the mind. At that point the mind is fixed on the object being noted, and his mindfulness is almost in step with the object of attention (such as the rising and falling of the abdomen). (In other words, the rising of the abdomen is noted at once, and so is its falling.)

The physical object that is noted and the mind that notes arise as a “pair.” In this process there is no person or individual; there is only the physical object noted and the mind that notes, arising as a pair. The meditator can actually experience this process. When noting the rising and falling of the abdomen, he can distinguish the rising of the abdomen as a physical phenomenon and the mind that notes it as a mental phenomenon. The same applies to the falling of the abdomen. The meditator will clearly realize that mental and physical phenomena arise simultaneously.

Thus the meditator will clearly know for himself that, in each noting, only matter (the body) is the object noted, and the mind gives it attention. This wisdom is called “knowledge of discerning mind and matter” (nāma-rūpa-pariccheda-ñāṇa), which is the beginning of insight wisdom. It is important to attain this wisdom correctly. As the meditator continues to note, this wisdom will lead to the wisdom that discerns cause and effect, called “knowledge of discerning conditionality” (paccaya-pariggaha-ñāṇa).

As the meditator continues to note, he can experience for himself that whatever arises soon passes away. Ordinary people think that mental and physical phenomena remain unchanged throughout one's life — that is, unchanged from childhood to old age — but in reality this is not so. No phenomenon is eternal and unchanging. All phenomena arise and pass away so quickly that it is faster than the blink of an eye. As long as the meditator keeps noting, he will come to understand this himself. He will be convinced that all these phenomena are impermanent. This conviction is called “contemplation of impermanence” (aniccānupassanā-ñāṇa).

This knowledge will lead to “contemplation of suffering” (dukkhānupassanā-ñāṇa), the experience that all that is impermanent is suffering. The meditator may also encounter various physical pains, which are the “aggregate of suffering.” This too is “contemplation of suffering.” Next, the meditator will be convinced that these mental and physical phenomena proceed according to nature, not according to anyone's wishes nor under anyone's control. They are not composed of a person or a self. This realization is “contemplation of non-self” (anattānupassanā-ñāṇa).

As he continues to meditate, the meditator will truly experience that all these phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and non-self, and he will realize nibbāna. All the Buddhas, arahants, and noble ones of the past realized nibbāna by this very path. All meditators should know that they are now on this path of “foundations of mindfulness” (satipaṭṭhāna), hoping to realize fully the path knowledge, fruition knowledge, and the Dharma of nibbāna, and to ripen their perfections (pāramī). They will experience the right concentration and wisdom that the Buddhas, arahants, and noble ones experienced. Since these experiences are ones they have never had before, they should rejoice in them.

Before long they will experience the path knowledge, fruition knowledge, and the Dharma of nibbāna that the Buddhas, arahants, and noble ones of the past experienced. In fact, these dharmas can be experienced within one month, twenty days, or fifteen days of meditation practice. Those whose accumulated merits are ripe can even experience them within seven days.

Therefore, the meditator should have faith that he will attain these dharmas within the time stated above, that he will eradicate the view of self and doubt, and that he will be freed from the danger of being reborn in the evil realms in future lives. He should continue meditating with this kind of faith.

blocks.text: A Brief Biography of Mahasi Sayadaw

inline.s: 1904: Venerable Mahasi was born in the village of Seikkhun in Myanmar. At the age of six he began studying the scriptures at a monastery in his village, and at twelve he left home to become a novice.

1923: In December he received full ordination and became a bhikkhu. In the following four years he successively passed the elementary, intermediate, and advanced government examinations in the Pāli scriptures.
1928: He went to Mandalay, where he received instruction from several learned bhikkhus.

1929: He was invited to Moulmein to teach the Dharma, where he studied the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta (the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness) in detail and became deeply interested in the method of insight meditation.

1931: He went to see the renowned Mingun Sayadaw and received four months of intensive meditation training under him. During this period of meditation, Venerable Mahasi attained complete insight wisdom.
1941: He passed the government examination for the title of Dhammācariya (Teacher of the Dhamma).

1945: Venerable Mahasi completed the Manual of Insight Meditation, which combines theory and practice to explain the method of the four foundations of mindfulness. One fifth of it was translated into English as Practical Vipassana Exercises.
1949: The Prime Minister of Myanmar,
U Nu (
U Nu
and U Thwin invited Venerable Mahasi to the meditation center in Yangon to give instruction in the method of insight meditation.

1954: Under state sponsorship, Burmese Buddhism held the Sixth Buddhist Council, at which Venerable Mahasi served as the final editor of the Tipiṭaka. In all, 117 volumes were edited, each of about 350 pages, and this historic task was completed in 1956.

1957: Venerable Mahasi was awarded the title of Agga-Mahāpaṇḍita (Great Wise One) by the government. This title is conferred on those who are proficient in the Pāli Tipiṭaka and have completed twenty years in the monkhood.
1982: On August 14, Venerable Mahasi passed away, at the age of seventy-nine.

Venerable Mahasi traveled abroad many times to propagate the Dharma, visiting Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, India, Sri Lanka, Japan, Indonesia, the United States, Europe, Singapore, Malaysia, Nepal, and other countries. Venerable Mahasi's
written works

are numerous — with English translations such as Practical Vipassana Exercises, The Fundamentals of Insight Meditation, Satipaṭṭhāna Vipassanā Meditation, and The Progress of Insight — and his lifetime achievements in propagating the Dharma have earned him a place among the great Buddhist masters of the present age.
